---
title: "Using the CLI"
description: "How to use Flower on the command-line."
order: 1
---

Flower is designed to provide a friendly user experience from
the command line. The CLI has commands for both viewing and building
documentation from a Data Package's metadata. The general pattern for
how to use Flower from the CLI is:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower COMMAND [ARGS] [OPTIONS]
```

To get started, try calling the program without any commands, arguments,
or options by typing `seedcase-flower` and pressing enter. This is the
same as invoking the `--help` flag and will show the following text:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower
```

## Viewing Data Package metadata

To view the metadata of a Data Package directly in the terminal, you can
use the `view` command like so:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower view
```

The `view` command displays the metadata in an easy to
read format that is optimized for display directly in the Terminal.

### Working with a Data Package in a custom location

By default, `view` looks for a `datapackage.json` file in the current
directory, but you can specify a different path if desired:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower view another/directory/datapackage.json
```

It also is possible to point Flower to a Data Package that is available
online. To do this, you can provide the full URL to the remote
`datapackage.json`, e.g.

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower view https://raw.githubusercontent.com/seedcase-project/example-seed-beetle/refs/heads/main/datapackage.json
```

For Data Packages on GitHub (like for the URL used above), you can use
the `gh:` prefix as a shortcut. For example, the long URL above can be
shortened to the following:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower view gh:seedcase-project/example-seed-beetle
```

<!--TODO should we include output for all of these commands? collapsed by default -->

### Styling the output

If you would like to customize the style of how the metadata is
displayed, you can use the `--style` flag. This option allows you to
format the output with any of [the built-in
styles](/docs/design/interface/outputs.html#built-in-styles):

<!-- TODO: point link above to guide for styles, or ref docs, not design -->

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower view --style terminal-simple gh:seedcase-project/example-seed-beetle
```

<!--TODO potentially change this depending on the name of this style when implemented -->

::: callout-important
If you have set the `style` option in a configuration file read by
Flower, you might be confused as to why it does not have an effect when
calling `seedcase-flower view --style ...`. The reason for this is that
the `view` command by design completely ignores any configuration read
from Flower's configuration file, even those with the same name as the
options passed to `view`. You can only configure `view` via command line
flags.
:::

For more details about what you can do with `view`, see `seedcase-flower
view --help`.

## Building documentation from Data Package metadata

In addition to viewing metadata in the terminal, Flower can organize
Data Package metadata into a set of plain text files. These files can be
used to build a documentation site which can make your Data Package's
metadata more easily discoverable and readable. Generating this set of
files can be achieved with the `build` command:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower build
```

When you run this command, you will see that there is one new file
generated: `docs/index.qmd`. <!--TODO Is this the correct location? -->
The `qmd` extension indicates that this file contains
[Quarto](https://quarto.org/)-flavored Markdown. While this is the
default text format outputted from Flower, you can change it by
specifying your own custom templates as detailed in [the configuration
section of this guide](/docs/design/interface/config.qmd).

<!--TODO change link when how-to section exists -->

### Changing input and output directory

By default, `build` will look for a `datapackage.json` file in the
current directory, but you can specify a different URI if desired (just
like with `view`):

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower build another/directory/datapackage.json
```

If you want the generated files to end up in another location, you can
use the `--output-dir` flag followed by a folder name. For example, to
create `my-dir/index.qmd` instead of `docs/index.qmd`, you would run the
following command.

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower build --output-dir my-dir
```

### Styling the output

Just like with the `view` command, the `build` command also accepts the
`--style` option, where you can choose to organize the metadata
according to one of the [built-in
styles](/docs/design/interface/outputs.html#built-in-styles).
<!-- TODO: point link above to guide for styles, or ref docs, not design -->
For example, to split the metadata for each resource in the Data Package
into its own file, you can run the following command:

```{.bash filename="Terminal"}
seedcase-flower build --style quarto-resource-listing
```

::: callout-important
If you try to use a style that worked fine with `view` for the `build`
command, you might be wondering why you received an error. This is
because `view` and `build` do not support the same styles, and you
need to make sure you use the correct set of styles for the respective
command.
:::
<!--TODO I think this approach with using the same option name but with different allowed values/styles could be quite confusing, particularly for new users. As previously, this creates the file `docs/index.qmd`, but now there is
also a separate file created for the data resource under
`docs/resources/seed-beetle-metabolic-rate.qmd`.
You can read more about the available default styles and how to create
your own custom style in [the configuration section of the
